title: Building an AI agent layer over multiple quantitative engines — how would you design the safety boundaries?
author: Rare_Reference3909
selftext:
Hi everyone,

We're building Nexyria, an independent project exploring quantitative intelligence across several domains.

Our current architecture includes three main areas:

- Nexyria Trader: algorithmic market analysis, signal evaluation, risk controls and automated execution.
- APEX Business: adaptive forecasting and evaluation against statistical baselines.
- Nexyria Sport: football predictions, confidence scoring and historical validation.

As these systems grow, we're facing a new architectural question:

How should AI agents interact with specialized quantitative engines without compromising their reliability?

We're considering a shared agent layer that could:

1. Read and interpret outputs from different engines.
2. Explain why a trading signal was rejected.
3. Analyze forecasting reports and their supporting evidence.
4. Detect anomalies, technical problems and potential improvements.
5. Propose research experiments without modifying production systems.

Our initial approach would be deliberately restrictive.

Agents would have read-only access to operational systems.

They could analyze information and recommend actions, but they wouldn't be allowed to modify algorithms, change risk parameters or execute trades autonomously.

For example, our trading system already operates in a live environment. We don't want an experimental AI agent interfering with its execution logic.

We're also considering separating the architecture into:

- A shared agent coordination layer.
- Domain-specific tools and permissions.
- Independent quantitative engines.
- An evidence and audit layer.
- Human approval for sensitive actions.

One challenge we're particularly interested in is avoiding the situation where an LLM generates a convincing explanation that isn't actually supported by the underlying quantitative system.

How would you approach this architecture?

Would you use one central agent with specialized tools, or several domain-specific agents coordinated by a supervisor?

And what safeguards would you consider essential before allowing an AI agent to interact with a live quantitative system?

We're still designing this architecture, so feedback from people working on agent systems, quantitative platforms or production AI would be very valuable.

comments.author: leroylabs
comments.body:
I’d use domain-specific agents behind typed, read-only tools, with the shared coordination layer limited to routing requests and collecting results. For Nexyria Trader, every explanation of a rejected signal should reference immutable evidence IDs for the exact engine output, risk rule, input timestamp, and software version. If a claim cannot resolve to that evidence graph, the UI should label it as an agent hypothesis rather than an engine finding.

Before connecting the live environment, test prompt injection inside forecasting reports, stale-data responses, cross-domain permission attempts from APEX Business, and audit-log failure. Human approval helps, but capability isolation should remain enforceable even when the supervisor is confidently wrong.

replies.author: Rare_Reference3909
replies.body:
Thanks for the detailed feedback. This is extremely useful.

I particularly like your suggestion of keeping the shared coordination layer limited to routing and aggregation, while domain-specific agents operate through strictly typed, read-only tools.

Your point about immutable evidence IDs is especially important for Nexyria Trader. We want explanations to be traceable to actual engine outputs, risk decisions, timestamps and software versions, rather than relying on an LLM to reconstruct what happened.

The distinction between a verified engine finding and an agent-generated hypothesis is something we definitely want to formalize.

We're also planning to keep the agent layer completely separate from LIVE execution while testing it.

The security scenarios you mentioned — prompt injection, stale data, cross-domain permissions and audit failures — would make a valuable adversarial test suite before any production integration.

Thanks again. This gives us several concrete requirements to incorporate into the architecture.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: you had the regime-switch prediction engine here a couple of weeks back, right? read-only is the right start, but "recommend actions" leaks once someone approves every suggestion on autopilot. I made Quantradin on that split: agents trade fake money and new positions need the owner's own key. free, quantradin.com. who approves a proposal in your live system, a person or a rule?

replies.author: Rare_Reference3909
replies.body:
Good question, and thanks for following up on our earlier discussion.

We're separating two different systems in Nexyria.

Our existing Trader LIVE engine operates under predefined execution rules and independent risk controls. It doesn't require manual approval for every trade that satisfies those previously authorized conditions.

The proposed AI agent layer is different.

Initially, agents would have read-only access. They could explain decisions, analyze evidence and suggest improvements, but they wouldn't have permission to execute trades or change production configurations.

If we later introduce actionable recommendations, the agent itself won't be the authority approving them.

Sensitive changes would require explicit human authorization, and any permitted execution would still be subject to independent technical safeguards.

We're also considering a separate paper environment where agents can evaluate proposals without interacting with real capital.

The main principle is that an agent's recommendation must never bypass the existing execution and risk architecture.

Your distinction between simulated activity and real-money authorization is a useful one. Appreciate the feedback!

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: keeping the rules engine and the agent apart makes sense. the place I'd watch is the seam: if the agent can ever edit the rules the live engine reads, the separation only exists in the diagram.

replies.author: Rare_Reference3909
replies.body:
That's an important distinction, and I agree.

Separating the agent from the execution engine isn't enough if the agent can modify the configuration or rules that the live engine consumes.

For Nexyria, we want that separation to be enforced at the permission and service level, not just in the architecture diagram.

The initial agent will have no write access to trading strategies, risk parameters, configuration files, execution services or anything that could indirectly affect LIVE behavior.

Any future configuration changes would have to go through a separate, explicitly authorized process.

We're treating the boundary between the agent and the live trading engine as a security requirement, not simply an architectural preference.

Thanks for highlighting that specific failure mode.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: enforcing it at the service level means nobody has to remember the rule later: the agent's account simply has no write on the config the engine reads. that's the version that survives a rushed Friday deploy.

replies.author: Rare_Reference3909
replies.body:
Exactly. That's the kind of enforcement we're aiming for: the agent's service account should be technically incapable of modifying anything consumed by LIVE, regardless of what the model requests.

We'll include explicit permission tests in the deployment process so that this boundary is verified rather than assumed.

Thanks again for the valuable feedback!

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Read-only first is the right call. For the explanation problem, one approach is to make the agent quote the exact log line, signal ID and number behind every claim, and have code check that the quote exists before the explanation is shown. I'd start with one agent that has narrow tools per domain, since a supervisor over several agents adds more places for things to go wrong. A few safeguards I'd want before any write access: a separate account with only the permissions it needs, a limit on how often it can call things, a full log of every request, and a switch that turns it off at once. Cymetica lets you connect your own AI agent and run it in paper mode first, which is a similar way to start with limited access.

replies.author: Rare_Reference3909
replies.body:
Thanks for the thoughtful feedback. You make a strong case for starting with a single agent and narrowly scoped, domain-specific tools rather than introducing a multi-agent supervisor too early.

I particularly like the idea of validating evidence references programmatically before displaying an explanation. Requiring signal IDs, exact engine outputs, timestamps and software versions could help prevent the agent from presenting unsupported interpretations as facts.

The operational safeguards you mentioned are also important for us: separate credentials, rate limits, complete audit logs and an independent kill switch.

Since our existing trading engine operates with real capital, the agent must remain completely isolated from execution permissions during the initial phase.

We'll incorporate these requirements into our architecture design and evaluate whether a single-agent approach is sufficient before adding more complexity.

Appreciate the practical suggestions!
